hints: Notice the axes: vertical is particle displacement away from or towards the source, horizontal is distance from the source to the right.
A compression means particles crowd together, so check whether particles just left and just right of a zero-crossing are moving toward each other.
Compare the slope at the two zero-crossings: one has displacement falling from away to towards with distance, the other has it rising from towards to away.
walkthrough: Identify the wave: energy transfer is to the right, and positive displacement means a particle is shifted to the right, away from the source.
Recall the test for a compression on a displacement-distance graph: particles on both sides must be displaced toward the point, giving high local density.

At the falling zero-crossing, just to the left displacement is positive so that particle is to the right of equilibrium, and just to the right displacement is negative so that particle is to the left of equilibrium.
Both neighbouring particles are therefore shifted toward the zero-crossing, so particles bunch together there.
At the rising zero-crossing the shifts are opposite, with left particle shifted left and right particle shifted right, so particles spread into a rarefaction.
The falling zero-crossing labelled with particles moving together is the centre of a compression. This is option B.

options.A: Point A is maximum displacement away from the source, so neighbouring particles are spread out, not crowded together into a compression.
options.B: At B particles to the left are displaced away from the source and particles to the right are displaced towards the source, so both sides move toward B and form a compression.
options.C: Point C is maximum displacement towards the source, where neighbouring particles are pulled apart to form the centre of a rarefaction.
options.D: At D particles to the left are displaced towards the source and particles to the right are displaced away from the source, so both sides move away from D and form a rarefaction.
